title: Romance Lied to You About Love. Jesus Tells the Truth.
paragraphs:
Romance Lied to You About Love. Jesus Tells the Truth.
Why Romance Movies Can Distort Marriage—and Why the Greatest Love Story Was Never About Finding "The One," But Becoming One in Christ
There is a quiet sermon preached every day that never comes from a church pulpit.
It streams into our homes.
It fills theaters.
It dominates social media clips.

It whispers through romantic soundtracks, dramatic reunions, passionate kisses, impossible coincidences, emotional speeches, and endings where every problem disappears because two people finally confessed their love.
Most people don't even realize they're being discipled.
Not by Scripture.
But by stories.

That doesn't mean every romance movie is evil. Many portray beautiful virtues like sacrifice, forgiveness, loyalty, courage, and hope. Those qualities reflect God's common grace wherever truth is found. Yet many romantic stories also reshape our expectations in ways that subtly pull our hearts away from God's design for marriage.
The danger is rarely obvious.
It is gradual.
It changes what we expect love to feel like.
It changes what we believe marriage exists to accomplish.
Eventually, we stop asking whether our expectations come from God.
We simply assume they do.
And then real marriage begins.
The butterflies eventually settle.
Conversations become ordinary.
Bills arrive.
Children wake up crying.
Health declines.
Forgiveness becomes repetitive.
The excitement fades into faithfulness.
Suddenly the marriage doesn't resemble the movie.
Many begin wondering whether they married the wrong person.
But perhaps they simply believed the wrong story.
Jesus never promised marriage would constantly feel cinematic.
He promised something infinitely greater.
He promised to transform sinners into saints through His grace.
That includes husbands.
That includes wives.
That includes every ordinary day.
From the very beginning, God revealed that marriage was never primarily about personal fulfillment.
It was about His glory.
Genesis records God's design before sin entered the world.
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." (Genesis 2:24, ESV)

The Hebrew expression דָּבַק (dāḇaq) means "to cling," "to hold fast," "to remain firmly joined." It describes covenant loyalty, not temporary emotion. It is the same word frequently used of Israel's call to cling faithfully to the Lord.
Marriage was never intended to rest upon fluctuating feelings.
It rests upon covenant.
The phrase בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (bāśār ʾeḥād) means "one flesh." This is far more profound than physical intimacy. It describes an inseparable covenantal union established by God Himself.
Movies often portray love as something you accidentally fall into.
Scripture presents love as something you intentionally live out.
Long after emotions rise and fall.
Long after the honeymoon.
Long after disappointments.
The New Testament deepens this vision.
Paul writes,
"Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her." (Ephesians 5:25, ESV)
The Greek word ἀγαπάω (agapaō) describes sacrificial, covenantal love that seeks another's good regardless of personal cost. This is not primarily emotional attraction. It is self-giving devotion.
Christ did not love His Church because she was flawless.
He loved her while she was still sinful.
"But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." (Romans 5:8, ESV)
Romance stories often climax with the wedding.
God's story begins there.
Marriage is not the finish line.
It is the training ground.
Every disagreement teaches humility.
Every apology teaches repentance.
Every forgiveness reflects the Gospel.
Every sacrifice mirrors Christ.
The greatest love story in history was never written in Hollywood.
It was written on a cross.
Jesus did not pursue a perfect Bride.
He redeemed one.
That changes everything.
Modern romance often teaches us to chase emotional highs.
Scripture teaches us to pursue holiness.
Those are not always the same path.
Peter writes,
"Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins." (1 Peter 4:8)
The Greek word ἐκτενής (ektenēs) means "stretched out," "constant," "persistent." It paints the picture of love that keeps reaching even when it becomes difficult.
That is the opposite of disposable love.
Marriage will expose selfishness you never knew you had.
It will reveal impatience.
Pride.
Control.
Bitterness.
Fear.
Not because marriage is broken.
Because we are.
God often uses marriage like a mirror.
Not to shame us.
But to sanctify us.
James reminds us,
"But be doers of the word, and not hearers only." (James 1:22)
Real marriages are built less by finding perfect compatibility and more by daily repentance.
This is why Jesus continually called people to deny themselves.
"If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me." (Luke 9:23)
The Greek word ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai) means "to utterly deny oneself." It is the opposite of modern culture's message that every relationship should revolve around personal happiness.
Christian marriage is not self-centered.
It is cross-centered.
Even the famous chapter on love refuses to romanticize it.
Paul writes,
"Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way." (1 Corinthians 13:4–5)
The Greek word μακροθυμεῖ (makrothymei) literally means "to be long-tempered." It describes enduring difficult people without quickly giving up.
That sounds far less glamorous than a romantic movie.
Yet infinitely more beautiful.
Because it reflects Christ Himself.
Marriage also points beyond itself.
Paul concludes his teaching with astonishing words.
"This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church." (Ephesians 5:32)
Marriage is ultimately a living illustration of the Gospel.
A husband imperfectly reflects Christ's sacrificial love.
A wife imperfectly reflects the Church's joyful response.
Neither picture is complete.
Both continually depend upon grace.
That is why every Christian marriage remains unfinished until glory.
The world's stories often end with, "They lived happily ever after."
The Bible tells a better story.
"They were forgiven."
"They kept repenting."
"They kept forgiving."
"They kept growing."
"They kept following Jesus."
That story is far more believable.
Because it is true.
Perhaps some reading this are disappointed.
Maybe your marriage feels ordinary.
Maybe you've been comparing your spouse to fictional characters.
Maybe you secretly wonder where all the excitement went.
Or perhaps you carry the wounds of betrayal, divorce, loneliness, abandonment, or broken dreams.
Jesus does not minimize those wounds.
He enters them.
The Gospel never promises that earthly marriages will always satisfy every longing.
Instead, it points us toward the Bridegroom who never fails.
Jesus Christ.
Every human marriage is temporary.
Christ's covenant with His redeemed people is eternal.
The longing underneath every love story ultimately points to Him.
The desire to be fully known.
Fully loved.
Fully accepted.
Fully secure.
No spouse can perfectly fulfill that longing.
Only Christ can.

If romance movies have shaped your expectations more than Scripture has, there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ (Romans 8:1). There is simply an invitation to exchange cultural fantasies for biblical hope.
The Gospel is not about finding someone who completes you.
The Gospel is about Christ making dead sinners alive, restoring what sin destroyed, and teaching husbands and wives to love one another with the same grace they themselves have received.
That is why our ministry exists.
Not to sell a fantasy.
But to point people to Jesus Christ—the only Savior who truly rewrites lives.
If this article helped you see marriage through the lens of Scripture instead of culture, don't let it stop with you.

Share what stood out most, or simply comment, "Christ is teaching me to love His way," if you desire a marriage shaped more by the Gospel than by the world. Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer needs today.

Marriage isn't transformed by one emotional moment but by repeatedly returning to God's truth. You may want to revisit these Scriptures when feelings fluctuate or expectations begin drifting back toward the world's definition of love.
Because the greatest love story was never about two perfect people finding each other.
It was always about a perfect Savior rescuing imperfect people.
That is the story worth giving your life to.
That is the story worth sharing.
That is the story worth living.
